claim: In two small studies of electronics troubleshooting (Rasmussen and Jensen 1974: 30 protocols; Burroughs 1979: two TV technicians, 40 trials), skilled troubleshooters usually opened with a functional search, ran many cheap good/bad checks, and localised by anchoring on a hunch; strict half-split was occasional (about 20% of check measurements in Rasmussen and Jensen) or absent (0 of 40 trials in Burroughs), while instructors report teaching it as a named strategy.
agent_test: Compare agent test count under free choice vs a code half-split on seeded single-fault chains at equal tokens.
audit_note: Samples are tiny (30 protocols; 2 technicians x 40 trials) and split-half is not absent: Rasmussen and Jensen report about 20% of 75 check measurements and some topographic search fields chosen by split-half; 'trained rule, not natural' is an inference, not a finding.
claim_before_audit: Skilled human troubleshooters rarely use textbook half-split. They open by function, run many cheap good/bad checks, and anchor on a hunch. Half-split is a trained rule, not the natural strategy.

claim: The terms topographic and symptomatic drift. In Rasmussen and Jensen 1974 topographic means position-wise good/bad scanning and the word symptomatic is absent; later reviews define topographic as search against a template of normal operation and symptomatic as matching abnormal patterns.
agent_test: None. Name our tests by the reference they need: normal-state, symptom-to-part map, or causal model.

claim: After a search routine fails, people repeat it with a small change (fixation) instead of switching method. Agents show the same loop: repeated actions track low accuracy in weak models, and repetition is a labelled failure in RCA runs.
agent_test: Add a code repeat-detector (same test class, same target, no new evidence) that forces a different test class; compare repeat rate and success at equal tokens.

claim: Half-split needs log2 N tests only for a single fault, linear chain, equal cost, reliable tests. One-step greedy information gain is exactly optimal at unit cost and equal priors and near optimal in practice, but constructed cases make greedy arbitrarily bad.
agent_test: Run greedy entropy selector vs exhaustive on small known-fault models; count tests to isolation.

claim: Under cost, rank candidate tests by probability per cost (single goal, independent sites) or by information per cost; prerequisites are grouped into blocs. Exact optimum is NP-hard, greedy is the standard design.
agent_test: Give agent a priced test menu; compare p/c-greedy order with model-chosen order on total cost to isolation.

claim: Unaided LLMs choose poor tests in some settings: ChatGPT in 8-candidate 20 Questions needed 7.24 questions vs 3.5 for the optimal questioner, kept asking after one candidate remained in 56.67% of games, and 39.44% of its second-turn questions had zero information gain; two Qwen3 models chose the highest-information question among their own considered candidates in only 19-36% of turns.
agent_test: Log fraction of agent tests with zero expected gain and tests after a singleton candidate set; target both near 0 with the code filter.
audit_note: ChatGPT numbers check (7.24 vs 3.5, 56.67%, 39.44%), but 'best split in a minority of turns' rests on two Qwen3 models picking the best of their own considered candidates (19-36%); ChatGPT in fact used halving questions more often than optimal (73.77% vs 57.14%).
claim_before_audit: Unaided LLMs choose poor tests: many questions carry zero information, they keep asking after one candidate remains, and they pick the best split in a minority of turns.

claim: Putting candidate tracking and expected-information-gain scoring in code, with the model only proposing tests and answers, raises success in closed-candidate games and dialogue troubleshooting (UoT FloDial GPT-4 43.7 to 67.3 percent, re-verified; BED-LLM +37.4 points in 20 Questions, re-verified; Battleship code layer). Evidence uses simulated answerers.
agent_test: Equal-token A/B: model-chosen next test vs model proposes k tests and code scores by gain on a seeded fault set.
audit_note: Minor: in UoT the LLM still simulates answers and partitions candidates, so scoring is only partly in code.

claim: The gain from EIG selection is not general: with large open hypothesis spaces and no clean split (AR-Bench), tree search, DPO and UoT gave small or negative gains. Whether a half-split scaffold helps depends on a closed, enumerable candidate set.
agent_test: Test the scaffold on a closed fault list and on an open one; report the gap.

claim: Asking the model to restate the live candidate set each turn shortens games and cuts contradictory questions (6.4 vs 7.24 questions, re-verified), but does not remove failure. In-context belief tracking is unreliable, so the ledger should live in code.
agent_test: Compare prompt-listed candidate set vs code ledger on redundant and post-singleton tests.
audit_note: Design conclusion (ledger in code) is inference; the 6.4 vs 7.24 and contradictory-question numbers (13.50 to 8.42) match, though trivial questions did not fall (25.15 to 26.78).

claim: Prompt-level fixes do not repair agent search errors: hypothesis templates and pitfall warnings were echoed but not obeyed (Kim 2026), and proactive CoT gave marginal gain (AR-Bench). Structural changes (passing raw code and errors between roles) gave firmer gains in steps than in accuracy.
agent_test: Pair each guardrail written as a prompt rule vs enforced in code; count violations.

claim: Extra reasoning has mixed value. It sharply improved questioning in partly observable 20-Questions style tasks (Qwen3-8B win rate 0.08 to 0.94) but did not improve fault isolation in HAProxy and cost about 10x output tokens.
agent_test: Enable reasoning only at test-selection step vs everywhere, equal tokens.

claim: Agents often reach a correct answer without a closed evidence path, and the main run-level failures are misreading returned data and incomplete exploration, not search order. Outcome accuracy overstates grounding (GPT-5 JRA 0.68 but evidence closure 0.21 and 0.15, re-verified).
agent_test: Score runs on evidence closure and path grounding as well as answer.

claim: Stopping is weak in both people and agents: keeping probing after decisive evidence, committing after one abnormal signal, over-diagnosing healthy systems (11 to 24 percent false fault reported), and people missing already-sufficient evidence.
agent_test: Add stop when candidate set is a singleton or all cheap checks pass; allow no-fault; measure false-fault rate and tests after sufficiency.

claim: More steps are not better for weak models: in Cloud-OpsBench the weakest models used 14-16 steps (about 3x the 5-6 of strong models) with repeated calls and low accuracy, GPT-3.5 in AIOpsLab gained nothing but token cost beyond 5 steps, and AR-Bench shows diminishing returns (+7.7% process score in rounds 5-10, +2.5% in rounds 20-25); stronger agents such as FLASH and ReAct did improve with larger step limits.
agent_test: Sweep step cap per backbone at equal tokens and find the knee.
audit_note: Numbers check, but 'more steps are not better' is too general: AIOpsLab shows ReAct and FLASH improved with more steps (FLASH peaked at 59.32% at a 20-step limit); only weak agents plateaued.
claim_before_audit: More steps are not better. Weak models use 3x steps for a fraction of accuracy; step limits beyond about 5 added only tokens for GPT-3.5 (re-verified); AR-Bench rounds show sharp diminishing returns.

claim: Greedy information selection can lose to random when its probability model is wrong. Spectrum-based diagnosis was worse than random on two programs with poor intermittency estimates; greedy has known pathological cases.
agent_test: Inject miscalibrated priors/reliabilities; check how far greedy falls below random.

claim: Using the half-split label did not by itself make repair faster in 8 student pairs. Model construction preceded the split in all five split-half pairs.
agent_test: Require predicted value per block before any split; compare vs no prediction.

claim: Teaching a fixed structured method with functional breakdown roughly doubled malfunctions solved by technicians (snippet only), while giving operators principles or procedures did not help diagnosing unfamiliar failures.
agent_test: Compare strategy encoded as code operator vs as text instruction.

claim: Binary search with a model as good/bad oracle is fragile: one wrong verdict ruins a bisect, and bisect needs deterministic tests and monotone failure. Use code tests as the oracle where possible.
agent_test: Inject oracle error rates into a bisect task; measure end-to-end success.

claim: Ordering by cost helped in a measured LLM loop: a panel with test-chooser, stewardship and budget tracker got 79.9 percent at $2,396 vs o3 78.6 percent at $7,850 on 304 cases. Numbers not re-verified (PDF damaged); hidden test set was 56 cases.
agent_test: Add price to test menu and a cheaper-equivalent check; compare cost to isolation.

claim: Retrieved past cases keyed by symptom transfer weakly; abstracted runbooks transfer slightly more steadily; evidence closure does not improve.
agent_test: Compare raw case retrieval vs abstracted rule memory on a held-out fault set.

claim: Structured symptom intake matters: vague tickets with no detail raised false faults to 47 percent and cut score from 0.82 to 0.50.
agent_test: Add a symptom-structuring step before the first test; compare.

claim: Topographic (normal-reference) search first to narrow, then symptomatic matching inside the region, is recommended by a review; coarse-to-fine has an overhead and does not always lower measurement count.
agent_test: Compare coarse-first vs cost-chosen grain on total tests.

claim: No published study compares an LLM agent own test order with a half-split or cost-weighted optimum on known faults by counting tests. Absence found by search only. Gap search 2026-10: still no direct study. Closest are fixed-budget accuracy tests (ACTMED d01) and Battleship (d13), neither counts tests to solve at equal tokens.
agent_test: Run it ourselves; it is the core test for this subfield.

claim: Code-side Bayesian test selection beats an LLM that picks its own tests at a fixed test budget on tabular diagnosis. The LLM prefers globally popular tests and does not tailor to the case.
agent_test: Seed faults; compare LLM free choice vs code gain selector on tests to solve at equal tokens.

claim: Most of the code-side gain in Battleship came from using answers (Bayesian move selection), not from scoring questions: question rule alone added +0.021 to +0.026 F1, full Bayes added about +0.4 F1 for weak models. Strong reasoning models gained little.
agent_test: Ablate: filter only, update only, scoring only; count tests to singleton.

claim: A zero-gain filter is cheap and works: redundant (EIG=0) questions fell from 18.5% to 0.2% (Llama-4-Scout) and 14.6% to 1.2% (GPT-4o) once code scored candidates. Filter and scoring were not separated.
agent_test: Add a filter alone and measure wasted tests.

claim: A stop rule on low expected belief change cut tests by about 50% with equal or better accuracy than a fixed 3-test budget; the stop rule was not separated from selection.
agent_test: Test stop on expected shift below threshold vs singleton set vs fixed cap.

claim: Planners that need an enumerable, eliminable candidate set fail on open answer spaces: UoT scored below zero-shot on AR-Bench, ToT and SFT were inconsistent, and rounds beyond about 20 added only +2.5% process score.
agent_test: Grow the fault list from small to open on a seeded system and find where the scaffold stops helping.

claim: Symptom matching fails on a rare fault that looks like a common one: experts used 39.33 tests against 13 for novices and spent 47.45% of tests on the look-alike part (N=3 vs 3, one circuit, no statistics). No measured switch rule exists.
agent_test: Trigger a normal-reference or split test after N failed confirmations of a symptom-matched hypothesis.

claim: Agents lack a no-fault exit. They report a false fault on 11% to 24% of healthy networks and spend most on vague tickets; timeouts were 9% of runs but 23% of spend.
agent_test: Add an explicit healthy-system checklist and no-fault answer; measure false-fault rate.

claim: SDBench numbers re-verified: cost savings came from asking cheap questions before costly tests with a veto role. Test price is in dollars and inference is negligible; for token-priced tests the relation is reversed and transfer is untested.
agent_test: Price tests in tokens and seconds; compare cheap-first vs EIG-per-cost order.

claim: A bisect with an LLM judge is all-or-nothing: base judge succeeded end to end on 74.2% of 32 questions, fine-tuned 80.6%. By own arithmetic that is about 94% per step if 5 steps, so verification of the last split is worth testing. No cheap-check result exists.
agent_test: Compare no check, vote of 3 on surprising splits, and boundary re-test.

claim: Structured troubleshooting training (strategy plus functional breakdown) doubled solved malfunctions in less time (abstract only; sample size unread). The effect cannot be assigned to half-split.
agent_test: Give the agent a functional breakdown and compare with strategy alone.

claim: BED-style inference selection is 25 to 36 times slower than a plain LLM questioner and gained little on 14B models (+1.8 to +4.2 points); an equal-token rule must charge for it.
agent_test: Count selector tokens in the arm total.
